display_title: Anthropic Warns of Self-Replicating AI Worms
display_title_he: אנתרופיק מזהירה מפני תולעי בינה מלאכותית משתכפלות
short_summary: Researchers at Anthropic demonstrated an autonomous AI worm that distributed its computing across smart televisions. The experiment has sparked fierce debate over whether adaptive malware poses an impending threat or merely an overhyped demonstration.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?

paragraphs: Amid pervasive debates surrounding hypothetical existential perils posed by artificial intelligence, Anthropic’s offensive research team—commonly termed a red team—recently demonstrated a practical cybersecurity hazard devoid of apocalyptic speculation. The researchers engineered an autonomous, self-replicating AI program capable of propagating across internet-connected household devices. By dispersing discrete fragments of itself across fifteen smart televisions, the malicious software operated cohesively, drawing a fraction of computing power from each device. Evoking the horcruxes of popular fiction that harbored fragments of a fractured soul, this distributed architecture exposes vulnerabilities in consumer hardware, where devices receive security patches far less frequently than laptops or mobile phones.

Unlike conventional malware that depends on human deception or phishing, worms propagate independently across networks. Historically, self-replicating code has triggered catastrophic disruption, spanning the pioneering 1988 Morris worm—which crippled early infrastructure by exploiting weak passwords and software flaws—to the sophisticated Stuxnet worm deployed by the United States and Israel against Iranian nuclear centrifuges, as well as destructive outbreaks like NotPetya and WannaCry that inflicted tens of billions in damages. The Anthropic researchers theorized that an AI-driven variant represents a distinct hazard because the model can continuously adapt, researching newly disclosed software flaws to compromise heterogeneous hardware. Although Anthropic acknowledged that effective worms require higher capability on less powerful hardware, they projected that current technological trajectories will render such functionality feasible by the year's end. Ariel Herbert-Voss, an early OpenAI specialist leading the startup RunSybil, noted that defensive systems remain unprepared for evolving threats that learn dynamically. Joshua Saxe, formerly in charge of Meta's AI security initiatives, similarly cautioned that cybersecurity professionals fail to treat these emerging risks with adequate seriousness.

Nevertheless, the immediate severity of such exploits remains keenly contested. A preceding study by University of Toronto researchers demonstrated an AI worm capable of traversing full-sized computers considerably faster than Anthropic’s television-based prototype. Jonas Guan, a doctoral co-author of that study, observed that while capabilities are developing swiftly, Anthropic’s television version advances slowly and produces detectable behaviors manageable through multi-layered defenses and routine digital hygiene, including two-factor authentication. Echoing this skepticism, SentinelOne research executive Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade dismissed the experiment as flashy stunt hacking, arguing it merely amplifies baseless doomsday narratives that falsely attribute independent willpower to AI models.

Meanwhile, former National Cyber Director Chris Inglis suggested that recent breakout events have settled questions regarding the technical plausibility of AI worms, noting they might ultimately serve defensive or benevolent purposes. Effective governance, however, remains hindered by political division: the White House has established only a modest review board, while members of Congress pursue conflicting legislative proposals. Observers also weigh whether dire warnings from commercial laboratories represent sincere vigilance, marketing maneuvers to inflate multi-trillion-dollar corporate valuations, or efforts to enact regulations that exclude commercial rivals. Still, as security specialist Gadi Evron argued when organizing an industry conference in San Francisco, even if corporate marketing exaggerates specific demonstrations, the underlying reality of the incoming AI storm will inevitably dwarf commercial public relations.

facts.fact: Anthropic's offensive red team created an autonomous AI worm that spread across 15 smart televisions by splitting its computing load.
Unlike traditional malware requiring human deception, worms spread independently; historical examples include the 1988 Morris worm, Stuxnet, NotPetya, and WannaCry.
Experts note that AI worms differ from older viruses because machine learning models can learn and adapt on the fly, researching new vulnerabilities.
Anthropic researchers estimated that running sophisticated AI worms across low-power hardware could become feasible by the end of the year.
Researchers from the University of Toronto previously documented an AI worm infecting full-size computers.
Skeptics like SentinelOne's Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade described the test as stunt hacking designed to feed alarmist doomsday narratives, noting standard security measures can stop it.

Former US National Cyber Director Chris Inglis stated that the plausibility of AI worms is already established, while conference organizer Gadi Evron warned that genuine risks exceed promotional hype.
